labor income (wage income, benefits, bonuses, severance pay, value of stock options)

registers.role: linkage (survey to register via anonymized CPR codes; spouse identification for household aggregation), controls (age, gender, number of children), sample frame for the survey
controls (highest level of education and resulting professional qualifications, coded as single-digit ISCED 2011)
variables_mentioned: highest level of education (ISCED 2011 single-digit codes)

registers.role: treatment (emergency-room visits by the respondent, their spouse or their children)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Consumer Expectations Survey (first module of Statistics Denmark's Omnibus Survey)
registers.role: outcomes (quantitative inflation forecasts and backcasts) and treatment (qualitative forecast of the household's financial position)
variables_mentioned: forecast of the household's financial position over the next 12 months

linkages: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey responses linked to the Danish administrative registry through unique anonymized CPR codes
individuals linked to spouses via the Danish Civil Registration System (CPR Registret); household income is the average of the two spouses when a spouse is present, otherwise the individual value
respondents linked to emergency-room visits of themselves, their spouse or their children in the Danish National Patient Registry
two purpose-built surveys (Denmark, May-June 2025, drawn from the population registry; United States, Prolific Academic, October 2024) are used for the mechanism tests and are not linked to registers

sample.universe: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey respondents aged 25-60 at the time of survey response, 2012-2019 (2013-2019 when inflation backcasts are the dependent variable), plus a register 'Population sample' of all Danish residents observed from 1991 onward who meet the same restrictions
sample.unit_of_observation: survey respondent interviewed in a given calendar month (person-year in the Population sample; elicitation, i.e. up to two per respondent, in the ER analysis; respondent-cue in the two supporting surveys)
selection_rules: monthly simple random sample of 1500 individuals drawn from the CPR register, invited through Digital Post, with reminders and telephone follow-up (average monthly response rate 64%)
restrict to survey respondents aged 25-60 at the time of survey response (55171 respondents satisfy the age restriction for 2012-2019)
exclude respondents with non-trivial self-employment income (more than one fourth of household income from self-employment in any year from four years before to one year after the interview)

exclude respondents who answered 'Do not know' to any of the key Likert questions, refused the quantitative inflation number boxes, or gave implausibly large numbers (forecast inflation above 100 percentage points)
exclude respondents with missing income or demographic information
trim all income changes at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
leaves 35050 usable responses for 2012-2019 (53367 for 2008-2019; 30752 for 2013-2019 backcasts; 48783 for 2009-2019 backcasts)

for the ER analysis: use 2008-2018, do not impose the demographic restrictions, and drop households with eight or more family ER visits in the sample period (177091 elicitations from 95637 survey responses)
sample.period: 2012-2019 main analysis; 2013-2019 for backcasts; 2008-2019 and 2009-2019 for the longest available series; 2008-2018 for the ER analysis; 1991-2019 for the Population sample
sample.n_observations: 35050 survey responses (main sample); 53367 (2008-2019); 30752 (2013-2019 backcasts); 48783 (2009-2019 backcasts); 62449159 person-years (Population sample); 177091 elicitations (ER analysis); 37440 respondent-cue observations (Danish supporting survey); 15230 (US supporting survey)
sample.n_individuals: 55171 survey respondents satisfy the age restrictions for 2012-2019, of whom 35050 responses are usable; only 467 respondents answer the survey more than once; 3744 Danish and 1523 US respondents in the supporting surveys

construction_notes: Recent household income change = log nominal household income in year t-1 minus log nominal household income in year t-2, with t the year of the survey response, so that recent income changes are fully realised before the survey response.
Future household income change = log nominal household income in year t+1 minus that in year t-1, so that past income is fully realised before and future income lies fully after the survey response.
Household income is the average of the two spouses' values when a spouse is present in the CPR register, and the individual value otherwise.

Total income is measured before taxes and labour-market contributions and includes labour income, public-sector transfers, property income and other taxable income attributable to the individual; it excludes imputed rental value of own housing, employer-administered pension contributions and lottery winnings.

All income changes are trimmed at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (labour-income and wealth changes trimmed analogously), and the trimming is retained even in analyses that do not involve income changes so that the sample is consistent.
Average past income level (the control) is the average log nominal income from year t-3 to t-5, chosen so as not to overlap the years used to build recent income changes.
Realized and forecasted inflation are expressed in percentage points, so the coefficients and bounds of Section 2 (inflation in decimal form) are scaled by 100.
Inflation forecasts and backcasts are elicited with a qualitative Likert question followed by a quantitative number box; a respondent who says prices will stay the same is coded as 0.

In the Population sample each individual-year is randomly assigned a calendar month, and inflation is computed over the 12 months following (or preceding) that month, to make it comparable to the survey sample.

Test 2' bounds are computed from the standard deviations sqrt(Var(Y)) = 0.00361, sqrt(Var(Xi)) = 0.577 and sqrt(Var(X)) = 0.009 for recent income changes (bound 0.0002, i.e. 0.02 in percentage points; 0.07 for the longest series) and 0.00361, 0.538 and 0.017 for future income changes (bound 0.00042, i.e. 0.042 in percentage points; 0.087 for the longest series).
Emergency-room visits come from the second, updated version of the National Patient Registry, available 1994-2018; the registry changed reporting system in 2019, which ends the ER sample in 2018.

no unemployment or leave in t-1 to t-2

population.selection: Monthly simple random sample of Danish residents drawn from the CPR register and invited through Digital Post (average monthly response rate 64%); respondents are then excluded if they have non-trivial self-employment income, answered “Do not know” to any key Likert question, refused or gave implausible (>100 pp) numbers in the quantitative inflation elicitations, or have missing income or demographic information; income changes are trimmed at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic household-level variation in administrative income (and in survey-elicited expectations of household finances) across repeated monthly cross-sections; the paper treats the regressions as descriptive joint-distribution tests of rational expectations rather than as a causal design

key_assumptions.assumption: Rational expectations (the null under test): the survey forecast (backcast) equals the Bayesian forecast given the respondent's information set plus idiosyncratic elicitation noise independent of that information set, of X and of Y
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as Definition 1 and equation (1); it is the null hypothesis the regressions are designed to reject

formal.as_written: Fi [Y |Ii ] = E[Y |Ii ] + ηi where ηi ⊥ Ii , Xi , Y

key_assumptions.assumption: Test 1 applicability: the household-level variable is in the respondent's information set, or more generally carries no information about actual inflation beyond that information set

formal.as_written: (Xi ⊥ Y |Ii )

key_assumptions.assumption: Test 2' signal structure (Assumption 1): the respondent's information is a single noisy signal of the partially observable component of the household variable, with mean-zero, mutually independent idiosyncratic noises independent of inflation and of the aggregate component, and E[Y|s_i] linear in the signal; plus |gamma| <= 1 or Cov(Z, gamma Y) >= 0
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as Assumption 1 and Test 2'; the resulting bound is shown to be small because most of the variation in household income changes is idiosyncratic

formal.as_written: Xi = Zi + γY + νi , si = Zi + δi and Zi = Z + ωi

key_assumptions.supported_by: stated explicitly at the end of Section 2

formal.as_written: (Xi ⊥ Y |Ii )

key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as Assumption 1 and Test 2'; the resulting bound is shown to be small because most of the variation in household income changes is idiosyncratic

formal.as_written: Xi = Zi + γY + νi , si = Zi + δi and Zi = Z + ωi

claims.statement: Respondents randomly interviewed in the month of a family emergency-room visit report higher inflation backcasts and forecasts.

treatment.label: I(Fam. ER visit in survey month)

register_source.value: Danish National Patient Registry (NPR), second updated version, emergency-room visits 1994-2018

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if any member of the household (the respondent, their spouse or their children) visited the emergency room in the calendar month of the interview.

timing.value: calendar month of the survey interview

register_source.value: Danish Consumer Expectations Survey (Statistics Denmark Omnibus Survey)

definition.value: Pooled quantitative elicitations of the inflation backcast (past 12 months) and the inflation forecast (next 12 months), in percentage points. An observation is an elicitation, so there are up to two observations per survey respondent.

timing.value: elicited in the survey month; the two pooled elicitations refer to the previous and the next 12 months

units.value: percentage points of inflation per family ER visit in the survey month (0/1 indicator)

magnitude.interpretation: the association with one additional family ER visit in the sample period is only 0.045, while the impact of a family ER visit in the survey month is approximately five times larger

estimand.target_population: Adult Danish Consumer Expectations Survey respondents 2008-2018 in households with at most 7 family ER visits over the sample period
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: the ER visit falls in the calendar month of the interview
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(family ER visit in survey month = 1)] − E[Y | do(family ER visit in survey month = 0)], conditional on the household's total number of family ER visits, demographics and calendar month

population.description: Full adult population of Danish Consumer Expectations Survey respondents, 2008-2018 (the main analysis's demographic restrictions are deliberately not imposed); households with more than 7 family ER visits over the sample period are dropped
population.selection: Monthly random sampling of survey respondents by Statistics Denmark; households with eight or more family ER visits in the sample period excluded; survey non-response is shown not to respond meaningfully to ER visits (Appendix Table B.29).

identification.source_of_variation: Random monthly sampling of survey respondents by Statistics Denmark, which makes the proximity between the interview month and a family emergency-room visit random, holding the household's total number of ER visits fixed

key_assumptions.assumption: Random monthly sampling: because Statistics Denmark draws a fresh random sample of respondents each month, whether a respondent is interviewed in the month of a family ER visit is random
key_assumptions.supported_by: the survey's monthly simple-random-sampling design

lhs: I(Fam. ER visit in survey month)
given: Total number of family ER visits in the sample period

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning on the household's general propensity to visit the ER removes the confounding between having an ER visit in the survey month and being an ER-prone household
key_assumptions.supported_by: controls for the total number of family ER visits entered linearly, quadratically and non-parametrically as fixed effects (and interacted with age) leave the estimate unchanged

implies_edges.from: Household propensity to visit the ER (total family ER visits in sample period)

key_assumptions.assumption: ER visits convey no price information: because emergency-room care is free for Danish residents, a visit cannot inform the respondent about prices
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as a design property of family ER visits

implies_edges.from: I(Fam. ER visit in survey month)
implies_edges.to: Price information in the respondent's information set

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential survey non-response: a family ER visit does not meaningfully change the probability of completing the survey
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table B.29 (an ER visit lowers completion by about 0.010, not statistically significant), plus a back-of-envelope bound in footnote 32

implies_edges.from: Survey completion

key_assumptions.assumption: Rational expectations (the null under test) implies that a proximate family ER visit has no relationship to the inflation forecast or backcast, conditional on the calendar month
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as the null hypothesis for this analysis

threats_discussed: survey non-response induced by a family ER visit
households with unusually many ER visits, for whom a visit is less unusual and less affect-inducing
the possibility that the ER effect is mediated by income changes (ruled out in Appendix Table B.30)
robustness_checks: controls for total family ER visits entered linearly, quadratically, as fixed effects, and as fixed effects interacted with age (Table 7, Columns 2-5)
demographic and time restrictions matching the main analysis (Appendix Table B.30, Column 1)
excluding households with 6+ or 10+ ER visits instead of 8+ (Appendix Table B.30, Columns 2-3)
controlling for recent and future income changes (Appendix Table B.30, Column 4)

formal.as_written: (Xi ⊥ Y |Ii )

key_assumptions.assumption: No causal interpretation is required: the tests are statements about the joint distribution of the household variable, actual inflation and the elicited belief, and hold whatever the direction of causality
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated explicitly at the end of Section 2

key_assumptions.assumption: Prior bias is not associated with income-growth trajectories, so the conditional association is not driven by persistent person-level optimism/pessimism about inflation
key_assumptions.supported_by: the coefficient grows rather than shrinks when demographic controls are added, and a placebo using income changes further in the past (Appendix Table B.5) shows no association

a “supply-side” view of inflation (people believing inflation is driven by negative supply shocks)
affective association without memory (Kahneman's “what you see is all there is”)
survey respondents reporting a moment of their belief distribution other than the mean
marriages and divorces creating mechanical household-income changes
income misreporting for the self-employed
